week.title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
week.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/
week.tldr: DexDuet learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterous RL policies from a single human demo with interaction rewards and an assisted curriculum.
week.summary: Object-tracking rewards let robots contact wrong parts or slide fingers. DexDuet adds two interaction rewards preserving human hand-object contacts, factorizes bimanual control into weight-sharing per-hand policies conditioned on each other, and uses assisted reference-state initialization. It is evaluated across four bimanual benchmarks.
week.why: Bimanual dexterity from human demonstrations with RL is exactly my core area.

week.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
week.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
week.tldr: iWAM conditions the policy on features from a single flow-video-model evaluation using a learned bidirectional flow map instead of generating future frames.
week.summary: Generating futures is too slow for control. iWAM inverts training futures into noise latents via flow-matching reversibility and learns a bidirectional flow map so one forward pass gives informative conditioning features. Recovers WAM generalization in sim and real at much lower inference cost.
week.why: A principled flow-map idea from Simchowitz's group linking generative-model theory and world-action policies.

week.title: OVOGO: Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
week.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning while inexpensive generative sampling supports policy optimization, providing an effective approach to experience-based post-training of flow-based VLAs.
week.tldr: OVOGO does offline RL for flow VLAs by separating offline critic learning from on-policy resampling of the generative process.
week.summary: Collecting new robot interactions for flow-VLA improvement is costly, but fresh generation trajectories can be resampled cheaply at replay observations. OVOGO learns a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic combining in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, then optimizes the flow policy on-policy over generated actions. It improves flow VLAs from logged experience.
week.why: Offline RL fine-tuning of flow-matching policies is a core RL+generative topic.

week.title: EgoStudy: How Does Scaling Egocentric Data Affect VLA and WAM Pretraining?
week.abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.
week.tldr: EgoStudy runs controlled experiments on how egocentric human data scale, diversity and processing affect VLA and world-action-model pretraining.
week.summary: The value of egocentric human data for robots is unclear due to embodiment gaps. Holding robot data fixed, they vary egocentric scale, diversity, processing and co-training for VLAs and WAMs. Diversity, trajectory alignment and detailed language matter most, with scaling effects differing between VLAs and WAMs.
week.why: Systematic study on learning from human egocentric data, central to dexterous data scaling.

week.title: DelayOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation from a Synchronous Teacher for Real-time Asynchronous Policies
week.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
week.tldr: DelayOPSD distills a synchronous flow-VLA teacher into an asynchronous delayed student on the policy's own rollouts for real-time execution.
week.summary: Asynchronous chunk execution conditions on stale observations; actions differ little on expert data but diverge on the policy's own delayed rollouts. DelayOPSD trains the delayed student, seeing an earlier frame plus pending actions, to imitate the synchronous teacher on on-policy rollouts. This recovers performance under latency.
week.why: Directly addresses real-time/asynchronous action chunking, a core interest.

week.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
week.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_0,π_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $π_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
week.tldr: JKO-GRPO augments Flow-GRPO for flow-matching VLAs with Wasserstein proximal (JKO) steps using transport targets from group advantages.
week.summary: Flow-GRPO and pi_RL reweight sampled actions by advantage but ignore distances between them. JKO-GRPO treats each state's action group as an empirical distribution, builds transport targets via a soft discrete c-transform of group-relative advantages, and regresses the deterministic flow sampler onto them alongside clipped Flow-GRPO without KL. It improves RL fine-tuning of pi0/pi0.5-style VLAs.
week.why: RL fine-tuning of flow VLAs with optimal transport is a core RL+generative-policy topic.

week.title: Distilling Touch into Vision-Only Policies for Contact-Rich Manipulation
week.abstract: Tactile feedback benefits contact-rich manipulation, yet deploying tactile sensors introduces additional hardware and maintenance requirements. Tactile experience can still provide effective supervision for policies that operate without tactile sensors at deployment. Tactile imagination methods such as TacImag remove this hardware dependency by predicting tactile observations, but retain a reconstruction stage whose errors can propagate into action generation. We present TacitTouch, a distillation framework that transfers tactile-guided behavior directly into a vision-only policy. The core shift is from "learn to imagine what touch would feel like" to "learn to behave as if you could feel touch": the student directly learns tactile-guided action patterns without reconstructing tactile observations. A frozen visuotactile teacher supervises the student's denoising predictions and intermediate action representations at the same noisy action and flow time. Training also uses demonstrated-action supervision. Deployment retains only the visual policy, with no tactile encoder, expert, or generator. Across four simulated UniVTAC tasks and four real-world tasks, TacitTouch achieves absolute improvements of 16.0% and 22.5% in mean success rate over vision-only control, respectively. The absolute gaps to the teacher using measured tactile input are only 2.0% and 3.75%, respectively. In robustness tests, it also outperforms TacImag, with absolute gains of up to 20.0% in mean success rate. Project page: https://pier-lab.github.io/tacittouch/
week.tldr: TacitTouch distills a visuotactile diffusion/flow teacher into a vision-only student by matching denoising predictions and action features.
week.summary: Tactile sensors add hardware burden, and tactile-imagination methods propagate reconstruction errors. TacitTouch has a frozen visuotactile teacher supervise the vision-only student's denoising predictions and intermediate action representations at matched noisy action and flow time, so the student behaves as if it could feel touch. It targets contact-rich manipulation without tactile sensors at deployment.
week.why: Combines tactile sensing, contact-rich manipulation and flow/diffusion policy distillation, all core interests.

week.title: DUO Policy: Bridging Human Video Coverage and Robot Precision for Fine-Grained Manipulation
week.abstract: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/
week.tldr: DUO Policy splits a skill into a human-video-pretrained hand policy for free-space motion and a robot policy for precise corrections, with a learned gate.
week.summary: Co-training on human and robot data treats sources as equally useful everywhere. DUO observes human data helps where precision demands are low, while robot data matters near precision-critical states; it uses a hand policy from human video, a robot policy from sparse in-hand data, and a gate learned from interventions. This enables fine-grained tasks like insertion with little robot data.
week.why: Clear insight on leveraging human video for precise manipulation, a core interest.

week.title: Ego2Real: Learning Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Visuo-Tactile Demonstrations
week.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations offers a scalable path toward robot skill acquisition. Vision alone, however, provides limited information about physical contacts and the demonstrator's force intent, leading to ambiguities in interpreting hand-object interactions. Capturing human touch via tactile sensing is therefore crucial for reliable human-to-robot dexterous skill transfer. We present Ego2Real, a framework that leverages egocentric demonstrations and tactile gloves to transfer bimanual dexterous manipulation skills to robotic hands. Ego2Real incorporates tactile supervision at two complementary stages: (1) tactile-guided hand-object interaction reconstruction, which uses measured tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry; and (2) contact-informed reinforcement learning, which translates human contact patterns into robotic contact rewards. By combining refined motion references with physical contact rewards during training, Ego2Real guides anthropomorphic robotic hands to emulate demonstrated contact behaviors while adapting to their own morphology and actuation. Experiments show that incorporating tactile supervision into both reconstruction and policy learning yields higher manipulation success rates, underscoring the importance of enriching egocentric demonstrations with tactile observations to improve their quality and transferability.
week.tldr: Ego2Real uses egocentric video plus tactile gloves to refine hand-object reconstruction and define contact rewards for RL transfer to bimanual robot hands.
week.summary: Vision-only human demos are ambiguous about contacts and force intent. Ego2Real uses glove tactile signals to refine hand poses and contact geometry, then converts human contact patterns into contact rewards for RL that trains anthropomorphic hands to track the reference while adapting to their morphology. Tactile supervision at both stages improves success rates.
week.why: Squarely in my human-to-robot dexterous transfer + tactile interests.

week.title: SOAR: temporal Structure-guided One-step Action generation for Robotic manipulation
week.abstract: Efficient robotic manipulation requires temporally coordinated actions with low inference latency. Multi-step diffusion and flow policies progressively refine action trajectories but require costly iterative inference, whereas one-step policies eliminate iterative trajectory refinement to reduce inference cost. We introduce SOAR, a structure-guided one-step generative policy that improves action quality while preserving one-step efficiency. SOAR predicts an observation-conditioned discrete cosine transform (DCT) representation of future actions, capturing temporal variations across multiple frequency bands to provide explicit guidance from key temporal structural information. Unlike velocity-parameterized one-step flow policies that recover clean actions indirectly from a predicted velocity field, SOAR directly generates clean action trajectories in action space. This aligns the model output with the executable control target and provides a direct interface for structural calibration. The predicted structure further corrects the generated trajectory according to their spectral discrepancy, without requiring an additional evaluation of the generative backbone. During training, the corresponding MeanFlow velocity is derived from the calibrated clean action and used for consistency learning, while an endpoint objective aligns training with the pure-noise condition used for one-step inference. Across 53 Adroit and Meta-World tasks, SOAR achieves 83.9% overall success with only 8.7 ms inference latency. When applied to the VLA model, $π_{0.5}$, SOAR further achieves 97.2% on LIBERO and 71.7% on RoboTwin 2.0. Real-world experiments and extensive ablations further validate its effectiveness and efficiency.
week.tldr: SOAR is a one-step generative policy that directly predicts DCT coefficients of action chunks to capture temporal structure.
week.summary: Multi-step diffusion/flow policies are slow, and velocity-parameterized one-step flows recover actions indirectly. SOAR predicts an observation-conditioned DCT representation across frequency bands and directly generates clean action trajectories, enabling structural calibration. It improves one-step action quality at one-step cost.
week.why: Fast one-step generative policies with action chunk structure are a core interest.

week.title: FunGrasp-Zero: Field-Conditioned Graph Attention Policy for Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Functional Grasping
week.abstract: Dexterous functional grasping is critical for robotic tool use, yet current dexterous hands exhibit substantial morphological diversity. This hardware heterogeneity makes cross-embodiment functional grasping a fundamental but largely unexplored problem. Existing functional grasping methods use retargeted hand poses as guidance, tying task representation to a specific embodiment and failing to explicitly capture object-centric functional contact intent, limiting generalization across hands. To address this, we propose FunGrasp-Zero, a reinforcement learning framework for zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping. Instead of relying on embodiment-specific joint configuration, FunGrasp-Zero captures functional intent via an object-centric, cross-embodiment-consistent contact map, adapted to heterogeneous hands through morphological mapping. We construct a hand-object potential field from mapped contact regions, yielding attractive and repulsive guidance vectors. A Field-Conditioned Graph Attention Network (FC-GAT) leverages these vectors to coordinate multi-finger motion across hands, while a potential field reward guides fingers toward target regions and penalizes non-target collisions to enforce functional alignment and stability. We further establish X-FunBench for cross-embodiment functional grasping, evaluating both physical grasp success and functional intent preservation across hands. Evaluated on X-FunBench, our unified policy, co-trained on four embodiments, achieves 86% average grasp success rate across five unseen hands on novel objects. Deployed on four unseen physical hands (Leap, Inspire, Sharpa, Wuji) for novel object grasping, the policy achieves 80% average success rate without fine-tuning. To our knowledge, FunGrasp-Zero is the first RL-based framework to achieve zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping across unseen hands in both simulation and the real world.
week.tldr: FunGrasp-Zero trains an RL graph-attention policy conditioned on object-centric contact-map potential fields for zero-shot cross-embodiment functional grasping.
week.summary: Functional grasping methods tie task representation to one hand via retargeted poses. FunGrasp-Zero represents intent as a cross-embodiment contact map mapped onto heterogeneous hands, builds attractive/repulsive hand-object potential fields, and conditions a graph attention RL policy on them. It enables zero-shot transfer to unseen hand morphologies.
week.why: Cross-embodiment dexterous functional grasping is squarely in my core area.

week.title: Dr. Grasp-RL: Diverse and Robust Dexterous Grasping via Reinforcement Learning
week.abstract: Human interaction with physical objects relies on a combination of dexterity and robustness. In robotic manipulation, dexterity requires not only flexible end effectors but also a diverse repertoire of manipulation strategies, while robustness requires closed-loop adaptation to disturbances and unexpected situations. Two prominent research directions in dexterous grasping have largely addressed these capabilities separately. Generative approaches model multimodal distributions to produce diverse grasp poses, but their reliance on open-loop execution can limit robustness. Reinforcement learning approaches learn closed-loop grasping policies, but can converge to a narrow range of successful grasping strategies, limiting behavioral diversity. We introduce a time-reversed curriculum with a coordinated reset mechanism that enables a simple MLP policy trained with PPO to capture multiple modes of the grasp-pose distribution while maintaining closed-loop control. Experiments demonstrate both diverse grasping behaviors and robust closed-loop execution. Trained on only approximately 400 objects, our policy further demonstrates strong generalization when evaluated on more than 20,000 unseen objects.
week.tldr: A time-reversed curriculum with coordinated resets lets a PPO MLP policy learn diverse multimodal dexterous grasps with closed-loop robustness.
week.summary: Generative grasp methods are diverse but open-loop, while RL policies are robust but collapse to few strategies. Dr. Grasp-RL uses a time-reversed curriculum and coordinated resets so a simple PPO policy captures multiple grasp-pose modes while remaining closed-loop. Experiments show both diversity and robustness.
week.why: Simple RL trick for diverse dexterous grasping; directly usable.

week.title: G0.7: Scaling Up a Fast World Action Model with Long Context
week.abstract: World action models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generators for robot control by jointly predicting future camera frames and actions, transferring physical priors learned from video into manipulation policies. However, generating future frames before every action makes test-time inference too slow for closed-loop control, while most existing policies remain restricted to short observation histories. Building on Fast-WAM, which showed that video prediction shapes policy representations during training so that future frame synthesis can be skipped at deployment, we present G0.7, a generalist world action model scaled along two axes: extending the context window from a single observation to up to five minutes of history, and scaling pretraining to a large-scale corpus of robot teleoperation and human egocentric (ego) video. Across public simulation suites and real-robot deployments, direct action decoding (Fast mode) matches imagine-then-act (IDM) inference from the same checkpoint while running in 60 ms per 16-step action chunk on a single RTX 5090 (7.6x faster than IDM) and supporting pause-free real-time chunking. Performance scales consistently with pretraining data, with human ego video driving the largest gains in out-of-distribution generalization: G0.7 achieves a 70.8 mean score across five simulation benchmark suites, 48% and 54% zero-shot pick-and-place success on Galaxea R1 Pro and R1 Lite, 96.7% in-distribution and 93.3% out-of-distribution success on video-conditioned in-context learning tasks, and 86.9% mean task progress across seven real-world post-training tasks including multi-minute box folding, drink preparation, and product bagging. Project page: https://www.galaxea-ai.com/model-g07.html
week.tldr: G0.7 scales a Fast-WAM world-action model to five-minute history context and large teleop plus egocentric-video pretraining, decoding actions without generating frames.
week.summary: WAMs are slow and short-context. G0.7 extends context to five minutes and scales pretraining; Fast mode matches imagine-then-act at 60 ms per 16-step chunk (7.6x faster) with real-time chunking. Human ego video drives the biggest OOD gains; 70.8 mean score on five sim suites and 86.9% task progress on seven real long-horizon tasks.
week.why: Combines long-context policies, world-action models and human video scaling — several of my interests at once.

week.title: Exploratory Midtraining for Robot Policies
week.abstract: Robot policies predominantly learn from human-collected data emphasizing competent behavior, limiting coverage of the low-level behaviors needed to support autonomous improvement. We study how a form of midtraining can be used to build coverage over diverse low-level behaviors that connect challenging states of the robot and its environment to states from which further progress is possible ("connected behavioral coverage"). We also examine how this coverage supports downstream adaptation and online improvement. To this end, we introduce $β$-Data, a dataset collected via adversarial teleoperation, where a human adversary reversibly perturbs the environment while a human operator continues toward completion without resetting. We relabel trajectory segments with local outcomes in natural language and finetune a pretrained policy conditioned on recent action history. The resulting policy exhibits sustained use of more low-level behaviors. Across manipulation tasks in simulation and on three real-robot platforms, our approach yields more favorable data scaling laws, better zero-shot generalization, and more effective use of additional rollout time than training on standard demonstrations. During online finetuning, these policies need fewer rollouts to collect successful experience and reach higher success rates, suggesting that midtraining can prepare robots for both more robust task execution and continued autonomous improvement. Our project page and robot videos are available at https://kshitiz-1225.github.io/exploratory-midtraining-robot-policies/.
week.tldr: Midtrains robot policies on adversarial-teleop data with local-outcome relabeling to build coverage of recovery behaviors for better scaling and online RL.
week.summary: Competent demos lack recovery behaviors. Beta-Data has a human adversary perturb the scene while the operator continues; segments are relabeled with local outcomes and a pretrained history-conditioned policy is finetuned. Across sim and three real platforms it gives better data scaling, zero-shot generalization and faster online finetuning.
week.why: A data-centric insight on preparing BC policies for RL fine-tuning — directly useful to me.

week.title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models
week.abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
week.tldr: Native LAM turns a pretrained video diffusion transformer into both inverse and forward dynamics, extracting compact latent actions via dynamics registers.
week.summary: Latent action models train IDM/FDM from scratch, trading reconstruction against latent capacity. Native LAM uses one pretrained video DiT as both, bridged only by learnable dynamics registers, trained on counterfactual pairs differing only in motion, so registers distill compact latent actions. They also propose a pretraining paradigm using these latents for action-free video.
week.why: Latent actions from video world models are a promising route to learning from human/egocentric video.

week.title: One Phase Is Enough: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Direct Visual Reinforcement Learning
week.abstract: Sim-to-real reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive robotic behaviors, yet deploying policies directly from vision remains challenging. A common approach first trains a teacher policy with RL using privileged state observations, then distills its behavior into a vision-based student via imitation. However, the resulting student can substantially underperform its teacher. Directly training visual policies with RL offers a promising alternative, but learning task-relevant visual representations from scratch can be sample-inefficient, making one-phase visual RL intractable. We propose DRIFT, a simple recipe for efficient one-phase visual RL using image observations available at test time. Our key insight is to use frozen, pretrained foundation vision encoders, allowing RL to focus on learning control from existing visual representations. Freezing the encoder avoids costly backpropagation through the vision backbone, while its pretrained representations enable real-world transfer from fast, rasterized simulation rendering. Under matched architectures, observations, and compute budgets, DRIFT outperforms two-phase distillation and achieves a 58.8% relative improvement in average real-world success rate across three manipulation tasks. Controlled simulation evaluations demonstrate that DRIFT's relative advantage grows from roughly 9% in-distribution to over 61% under out-of-distribution shifts, suggesting that stronger generalization contributes to superior real-world transfer. Project website: https://jmarangola.github.io/one-phase-visual-rl/
week.tldr: DRIFT trains vision-based sim-to-real RL policies in one phase using frozen pretrained vision encoders instead of teacher-student distillation.
week.summary: Teacher-student distillation for visual sim-to-real often leaves the student well below the teacher. DRIFT freezes a pretrained foundation vision encoder so RL only learns control, avoiding backprop through the backbone and enabling transfer from fast rasterized rendering. It yields a 58.8% relative real-world success improvement over two-phase distillation on three tasks, with the gap growing to 61% under OOD shifts.
week.why: A simple recipe me could use to skip teacher-student distillation in sim-to-real manipulation, including dexterous settings.

week.title: Reinforcing Diffusion Models by Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching
week.abstract: Forward diffusion reinforcement learning (RL)---enabling deterministic ODE sampling without trajectory backpropagation---has grown increasingly popular for efficiently aligning diffusion models. However, we reveal that existing methods essentially rely on signed reward-weighted regression (RWR), regressing the trainable policy velocity onto rollouts from a behavior distribution. Unbiased baseline subtraction implicitly assumes that the policy velocity equals the behavior marginal velocity---an idealized assumption violated under classifier-free guidance (CFG) rollouts, offline/off-policy updates, and imperfect online self-consistency. This behavior--policy mismatch breaks baseline invariance and injects baseline-induced gradient drift, destabilizing training. To resolve this issue, we propose Instantaneous Trajectory Distribution Matching (iTDM), taking the infinitesimal limit of Trajectory Distribution Matching toward a time-local reward-guided target via the posterior-score identity to yield a sample-level gradient anchored at the behavior velocity without learning an additional reward-tilted target score. Tracking this velocity with an online auxiliary denoiser guarantees exact baseline invariance at the auxiliary optimum, effectively suppressing baseline drift across both online and offline RL. Extensive experiments across compositional generation, text rendering, and preference alignment show that iTDM achieves state-of-the-art in-domain and out-of-domain performance across group-wise online/offline RL and pairwise offline RL. Notably, on the challenging GenEval2 benchmark, iTDM converges nearly 3\times faster than competing methods while scaling smoothly to 0.87 without collapse. Furthermore, iTDM scales effectively to the 5.6B FLUX.3 model, achieving better performance across both in-domain and unseen metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/Luo-Yihong/iTDM
week.tldr: iTDM identifies baseline-induced gradient drift in forward diffusion RL and fixes it via instantaneous trajectory distribution matching.
week.summary: Forward diffusion RL methods are signed reward-weighted regression whose baseline subtraction assumes policy velocity equals behavior marginal velocity, violated under CFG, off-policy updates and imperfect self-consistency. iTDM takes the infinitesimal limit of trajectory distribution matching to remove this mismatch. It stabilizes diffusion RL alignment.
week.why: Clear theoretical insight into RL for diffusion/flow models, transferable to diffusion policies.

week.title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
week.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.
week.tldr: Shows classifier-free guidance activates otherwise harmless solenoidal score errors, analyzed via weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition.
week.summary: Solenoidal score-error components don't affect their own reference density, but CFG's guided density differs, so these errors become active. The paper quantifies the activated error field, its dependence on guidance strength, and links it to generated densities via ODE/Feynman-Kac; for Gaussian mixtures it explains most of the KL error.
week.why: Rigorous guidance theory explaining a hidden failure mode of CFG, squarely in my generative-theory interests.

week.title: Demystifying Classifier-Free Guidance for Auto-Regressive Image Generation
week.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) has been widely adopted in autoregressive (AR) models for high-quality image generation. Despite its strong empirical performance, its mechanism in AR models remains unclear. This paper demystifies the mechanism of CFG through both empirical and theoretical studies. By examining the top-ranked semantics of different components in CFG, we show that texture information is primarily encoded in the difference between the conditional and unconditional logits, whereas both logits share previous-token repetition as their leading semantics. This strong repetition semantics obscures the desired texture information, causing greedy decoding from the conditional logits alone to produce nearly pure-color images. Through a training-dynamics analysis of shallow transformers, we prove that this shared repetition semantics does not arise from limitations or failures of pretraining, but instead originates from the texture sparsity of images. We further show that CFG improves generation quality by rectifying this repetition bias during inference. Motivated by the shared semantics between conditional and unconditional logits, we propose Attention Weight Reuse (AttnReuse), which reuses intermediate attention computations from the conditional-logit forward pass to accelerate the unconditional-logit computation. AttnReuse reduces about $25\%$ of attention computation with little performance degradation across different models.
week.tldr: Explains CFG in autoregressive image models: shared logits encode token repetition, while the CFG difference carries sparse texture information.
week.summary: CFG works in AR image models but its mechanism is unclear. They show texture info lives in the conditional-unconditional logit difference while both logits are dominated by previous-token repetition, and prove via training dynamics of shallow transformers that this stems from texture sparsity. CFG thus removes shared repetition semantics.
week.why: Rigorous guidance theory; relevant to generative-model understanding, though for AR not diffusion.

week.title: Scalable Beckmann Maps Improve One-step Generation
week.abstract: Beckmann Transport Models (BTM) learn one-step generative maps end-to-end from data, without a teacher, a distillation stage, or pretrained features. We introduce Scalable Beckmann Maps (SBM), which bring to BTM the two ingredients behind the quality of modern multistep generators: classifier-free guidance (CFG) and a training recipe that scales, while keeping sampling at a single network evaluation. CFG combines conditional and unconditional velocity or score predictions, which a Beckmann map does not have. Our guidance rests on one observation: the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, to which CFG applies as it does to a velocity. With exact denoisers this gives guided BTM. In practice we substitute the map's own conditional and null predictions for the denoisers, which requires no additional network and introduces a bias that we characterize. We show that the guided update is consistent with a guided conservation equation, and that guidance can move the boundaries between basins, sending more noise to the modes a condition favors. Trained from scratch in the latent of a representation autoencoder, SBM reaches a one-step FID of 1.6 on ImageNet 256x256 without a teacher or a feature loss, outperforming the Improved-MeanFlow baseline with 3.2x fewer FLOPs. In text-to-image generation it reaches a GenEval score of 0.86 with one network evaluation. As a world model, where we train without guidance, the recipe alone outperforms DriftWorld on all five metrics of two robot-manipulation benchmarks, with 1.9-2.8x less training compute and no pretrained auxiliary feature encoder.
week.tldr: Adds classifier-free guidance and a scalable training recipe to Beckmann Transport Models for teacher-free one-step generation.
week.summary: Beckmann Transport Models learn one-step generative maps without distillation but lacked CFG and scalable training. SBM observes that the BTM current is a positive multiple of an autonomous denoising field, so CFG can be applied using the map's own conditional/null predictions, with characterized bias. Guidance provably shifts basin boundaries toward condition-favored modes while keeping single-NFE sampling.
week.why: One-step generation theory with guidance is directly in my generative-model interests and relevant to fast policies.

week.title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
week.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.
week.tldr: TacInno supervises visuotactile VLAs with discrete codes of 'tactile innovation' that vision and actions cannot predict.
week.summary: Much tactile change is predictable from vision and actions, so VLAs ignore touch; a tokenizer conditioned on vision and actions compresses only the unexplained future tactile change into codes the policy learns to predict as an auxiliary target. It gets 87.5% on six sim and 70.5% on four real tasks, +10.7/+9.0 over the best visuotactile baseline.
week.why: Clever insight on why tactile input is underused, applicable to tactile dexterous policies.

week.title: Coherent Moment Propagation: Epistemic Uncertainty for Pre-trained Robot Policies
week.abstract: Flow matching policies underpin the state-of-the-art in robot learning, with impressive results ranging from long-horizon planning to dexterous manipulation. However, they provide no measure of whether their predicted commands can be trusted, particularly in novel situations outside their training set. Epistemic uncertainty reflects uncertainty about the model's weights and quantifies this ignorance, but calculating it at inference time from a flow matching policy is not trivial. Actions are produced by an ODE solver, requiring uncertainty to be propagated through the entire integration process. BayesDiff addresses this problem for diffusion models by propagating the mean and variance of the state through the denoising chain under a last-layer Laplace posterior approximation, but it severely underestimates the epistemic uncertainty. In this paper we: i) prove that, for flow matching and diffusion ODEs, BayesDiff's total variance decays at rate $O(1/T)$ as the number of Euler steps $T$ used by the solver increases; ii) introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters that fix this problem by carrying the cross-covariance between state and weights; and iii) widen the last-layer posterior with observation embeddings the policy already computes, improving uncertainty estimates without retraining for CoMP and several test-time estimators alike. We demonstrate these benefits on three manipulation benchmarks with applications in failure detection and demonstration selection for fine-tuning, where CoMP corrects BayesDiff's variance collapse while matching or outperforming several uncertainty estimators.
week.tldr: CoMP propagates epistemic uncertainty through flow-matching policy ODEs correctly, fixing BayesDiff's O(1/T) variance collapse.
week.summary: The authors prove BayesDiff's variance decays as O(1/T) with Euler steps, introduce EKF/UKF-style recursions carrying state-weight cross-covariance, and widen last-layer posteriors with observation embeddings. On three manipulation benchmarks it improves failure detection and demo selection.
week.why: Rigorous uncertainty estimation for pretrained flow policies.

week.title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
week.abstract: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. In language models, a sink is a token with high incoming attention, a small value, and little effect on the output. We test whether that profile holds, not the horizon rule, in one $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks. The two endpoints receive 5.4% of action-key mass, 1.4 percentage points above their uniform share, and rotary positional encoding produces this excess: directly in shallow layers and through upstream action-token RoPE deeper in the network. The endpoints do not fit the sink profile. Their value norms stay near the action-token mean in all 18 layers. On 250 paired episodes, masking them or zeroing their values changes success by less than 4 points, and replacing their value directions with those of another observation lowers it by 3.2 to 7.2 points across three donors, whereas the same replacement on two non-endpoint tokens in the executed prefix lowers it by 28.4 points. The token that does fit the sink profile on mass and value norm is the prefix BOS; on this checkpoint, zeroing its value raises success in two paired runs, by +13.2 points (95% CI [+7.0, +19.4]) and +6.0 points ([+0.2, +11.8]). Inside the action chunk, a relative-offset routing profile estimated on other tasks keeps 75% of action-token spread and keeps closed-loop success on three held-out tasks (42.7% against a 38.7% baseline), while uniform or shuffled routing drops success to 3-4%. High attention mass alone does not tell what a token does.
week.tldr: Shows the 'radial action sink' endpoint attention in pi0.5 is a RoPE artifact, not a true sink, via value-norm and ablation analysis.
week.summary: Prior work treats high attention on first/last action tokens of flow VLAs as an attention sink. Analyzing a pi0.5 checkpoint on five RoboCasa tasks, the endpoints get only 1.4pp excess attention from RoPE, have normal value norms, and masking them changes success <4 points, while swapping values of executed-prefix tokens drops success 28.4 points. The token that matters is elsewhere in the executed prefix.
week.why: A careful mechanistic 'why' analysis of action chunking in flow VLAs, exactly my preferred style.

week.title: iMFPO: Improving Mean Flow Policy Optimization with Drift-Aware Velocity Alignment for Embodied Control
week.abstract: Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging. In particular, evolving action distributions during online reinforcement learning may introduce inconsistencies between instantaneous-velocity learning and interval-averaged action generation. To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. A shared interval-conditioned actor supports instantaneous-velocity supervision and interval-averaged action generation. JVP-corrected velocity regression is jointly optimized with reward-driven policy objectives, with action-level guidance from a frozen PPO teacher during training. At inference, iMFPO directly generates actions through interval-averaged velocity prediction, achieving one-step control without iterative flow integration. Across Go2, G1, H1, and Spot, zero-latent evaluation yields mean returns of 35.69, 34.44, 416.23, and 29.86. On Go2, action-generation latency drops from 15.57 ms to 0.41 ms relative to 64-step RFPO. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/iMFPO. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/iMFPO.
week.tldr: To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment.
week.summary: To address this challenge, we propose iMFPO, a one-step generative policy optimization framework with decoupled velocity learning and drift-aware velocity alignment. Flow-based generative policies offer expressive action modeling for embodied control, yet achieving efficient one-step generation under reward-driven policy optimization remains challenging.

week.title: DexWAC: A Unified World-Actor-Critic Model for Dexterous Robot Manipulation
week.abstract: Robot demonstrations provide more than actions to imitate: they reveal how actions change the world and how those changes contribute to task success. Recent world-action models (WAMs) extend vision-language-action (VLA) models with the first signal by jointly predicting actions and future observations, yet this predictive ability serves only as an auxiliary loss for policy learning. Meanwhile, most policy improvement methods learn dynamics and values in separate models, increasing training overhead and limiting representation sharing between these complementary objectives. We introduce DexWAC, a unified world-actor-critic model that jointly learns an actor, an action-conditioned world model, and a bootstrapped critic in a single robot pretraining stage. Our key insight is that visual prediction encourages control-relevant features, while value supervision promotes task-relevant representations; together, they shape a representation suited to policy learning. Built on an image-editing backbone, DexWAC predicts, for each action chunk, the visual latent and proprioception at its endpoint together with its reward and continuation, so the world model alone efficiently yields complete imagined transitions without generating intermediate video frames. After adapting the world model and critic on real rollouts, we improve the pretrained actor through either PPO on imagined rollouts or critic-guided best-of-$N$ selection. DexWAC surpasses the large-scale pretrained VLA and WAM baselines in simulation and achieves 75% average success on two real-world tasks, compared with 45% for $π_{0.5}$. Its world model is more accurate and faster than video-based baselines, and ablations confirm that learning dynamics and value together improves the policy.
week.tldr: DexWAC jointly learns actor, action-chunk-level world model and critic in one pretraining stage, then improves the policy via imagined PPO or best-of-N.
week.summary: Instead of separate dynamics and value models, DexWAC uses an image-editing backbone to predict, per action chunk, the endpoint visual latent, proprioception, reward and continuation. After adapting on real rollouts, the actor improves with PPO in imagination or critic-guided best-of-N. Achieves 75% real-world success on two dexterous tasks vs 45% for pi0.5.
week.why: Connects world-action models, critics and RL fine-tuning for dexterous policies — relevant to several of my interests.

week.title: ViTacLab: Physically Consistent Visuo-Tactile Simulation, Benchmarking, and Representation Learning for Robotic Manipulation
week.abstract: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich robotic manipulation, but existing visuo-tactile simulators trade physical fidelity for scalability, and benchmarks largely focus on two-finger grippers. We present ViTacLab, a framework comprising ViTacSim, ViTacBench, and ViTacPolicy. ViTacSim uses a tri-modal tactile primitive: a global sparse contact-force lattice, a local dense force array, and tactile images. Anchored to PhysX contact-solver outputs, it corrects normal inconsistency through local stiffness alignment and reconstructs tangential forces under decoupled slip-stick regimes while preserving GPU parallelism. A joint projection preserves the sparse wrench and enforces local friction cones. ViTacBench spans parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and bimanual systems, with tasks ranging from vision-dominant to tactile-dominant regimes. ViTacPolicy aggregates variable numbers of heterogeneous tactile inputs using spatial-pose embeddings and a Transformer, and aligns force-array and tactile-image modalities through a two-stream VQ-VAE with a shared codebook. Controlled Hertzian-reference indentation and real-sensor sliding tests reduce normal and tangential force RMSE from 2.31 and 1.85 N to 0.42 and 0.53 N, respectively. Throughput reaches 2,482.9 tactile-pipeline FPS at 256 parallel environments. Simulation and real-world experiments show gains on several contact-rich tasks, while low absolute success on tactile-dominant tasks highlights the remaining difficulty of purely tactile control.
week.tldr: ViTacLab provides a physically consistent GPU visuo-tactile simulator, a benchmark spanning grippers to dexterous hands, and a tactile policy architecture.
week.summary: Existing tactile simulators trade fidelity for scale and target grippers. ViTacSim anchors tri-modal tactile primitives to PhysX contact outputs, correcting normal and tangential forces (RMSE 2.31/1.85 N to 0.42/0.53 N) at ~2,483 FPS over 256 envs; ViTacBench covers grippers, hands and bimanual setups; ViTacPolicy fuses heterogeneous tactile inputs via a shared-codebook VQ-VAE. Tactile-dominant tasks remain hard.
week.why: Potentially useful infrastructure for my tactile dexterous sim-to-real work.

week.title: Two-Stage Post-Training for Flow-Based Embodied Foundation Models
week.abstract: Large-scale pretraining provides embodied models with general capabilities, but reliable task execution still requires post training. In multitask settings, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) faces distribution mismatch between training and deployment, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) is limited by sparse rewards and uneven learning progress across tasks. Multi-teacher on policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates expert capabilities through dense supervision on the model's own trajectories, but achieving performance beyond the teachers remains challenging. We propose a two-stage post training framework for flow-based embodied models, constructing distillation objectives from the velocity regression formulation of conditional flow matching. Stage 1 efficiently consolidates expert capabilities through MOPD. Stage 2 combines RL with teacher distillation that weights velocity errors according to the sampling noise, where distillation is restricted to failed trajectories to supplement sparse rewards with dense guidance without directly constraining successful behaviors. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that the framework outperforms joint SFT and exceeds the corresponding teachers' aggregate success rates. Sample efficiency comparisons show higher success rates than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.
week.tldr: Two-stage post-training for flow-based VLAs: multi-teacher on-policy distillation, then RL plus noise-weighted velocity distillation on failed trajectories.
week.summary: Builds distillation objectives from the conditional flow-matching velocity regression. Stage 1 consolidates experts via on-policy distillation; Stage 2 combines RL with teacher distillation weighted by sampling noise and applied only to failures. Exceeds teachers' aggregate success and is more sample-efficient than direct RL.
week.why: Directly on RL fine-tuning of flow policies, a core interest.

week.title: VeriTouch: Verified Visuo-Tactile World Models that Improve Robot Policy Learning
week.abstract: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.
week.tldr: VeriTouch generates synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories with a joint video-tactile world model and verifies them for policy learning.
week.summary: Visuo-tactile data is costly to collect. VeriGen jointly generates dual-view videos and tactile sequences from an initial image and instruction using a tactile expert plus pretrained video model, and VeriEval filters for visual and tactile plausibility. Verified synthetic data improves visuo-tactile policy learning.
week.why: Synthetic tactile data from video generation (DreamGen-style) matches both tactile and world-model interests.

week.title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
week.abstract: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.
week.tldr: DexLatentWorld learns a 3D cross-embodiment latent-action world model from retargeted human point-cloud demos and plans with MPC in latent space.
week.summary: World models need action labels and are embodiment-specific. A contrastive objective learns continuous latent actions from point clouds of retargeted human demos; MPC samples latent actions predicting particle futures, and robot commands are recovered from predicted geometry without an embodiment decoder. This enables zero-shot manipulation on unseen embodiments.
week.why: Human-demo-driven cross-embodiment world models for dexterous manipulation.

week.title: Force2Act: A Force-Aware Visuomotor Policy for Generalizable Compliant Robot Manipulation
week.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to regulate the force it applies, not only where it moves. Existing force-aware policies learn this force from demonstrations and therefore reproduce the force levels they were trained on, which fails once the interaction demands more force than any demonstration. We present Force2Act, a hybrid force-position policy built on two complementary mechanisms. A global force policy plans the motion and the interaction force once per action chunk, with force represented relative to the measured interaction, so that the planned force scales with the load. Between planning steps, a reactive compliance policy, termed Mixture of Force Experts, identifies at every control step the force expert that governs the interaction and regulates the force through it, so that the contact holds when it changes within a chunk. We further introduce Force2Act-Bench, a simulation benchmark of five contact-rich tasks that gives the community a common and repeatable way to test force-aware policies and measure how well they regulate the interaction force. Force2Act achieves an overall success rate of 93.8%, compared with 77.0% for the strongest baseline, and its reactive regulation reduces the failures on block pivoting from 30 to 10 of 150 trials. On a real robot, Force2Act reaches an average success rate of 94.2% over four tasks, against at most 27.5% for the baselines.
week.tldr: Force2Act plans motion and relative force per action chunk and uses a mixture of force experts for reactive compliance within chunks.
week.summary: Force-aware policies reproduce demonstrated force levels and fail when more force is needed. Force2Act plans motion and force relative to measured interaction once per chunk and uses a Mixture of Force Experts to regulate force each control step. It introduces Force2Act-Bench with five contact-rich tasks.
week.why: Combines action chunking with reactive force control for contact-rich manipulation.

month.title: ALOHA Lightning: Learning Fast and Precise Manipulation
month.abstract: Learning from human demonstrations has enabled robots to acquire a wide range of manipulation skills, but learned policies typically execute far slower than ordinary humans. This speed gap is mainly due to lack of an interface for collecting demonstration data at high speed, and the difficulty in training policies that can robustly execute high-speed motions. In this paper, we present ALOHA Lightning (Flash ALOHA), a system for learning fast and precise robotic manipulation. Our system uses kinesthetic teaching to intuitively collect near-human-speed demonstrations on a backdrivable bimanual platform, yielding natural and fast trajectories. We also present a learning pipeline that enables smooth high-speed execution through test-time action smoothing and aligns the visual data distribution between data collection and deployment with masking. Given 50 demonstrations for each task, ALOHA Lightning autonomously completes bimanual tasks such as ball tossing and catching, folding shorts, battery insertion, and bussing tables for over 80% success rates while close to human speed. Project website: https://flash-aloha.github.io/
month.tldr: ALOHA Lightning collects near-human-speed kinesthetic demos and learns fast precise bimanual policies with action smoothing and visual masking.
month.summary: Policies are usually much slower than humans; using a backdrivable bimanual platform for fast kinesthetic demos, test-time action smoothing, and masking to align visual distributions, it achieves >80% success near human speed on tossing/catching, folding, battery insertion, and bussing with 50 demos each.
month.why: Strong real-robot results on high-speed imitation from Finn's lab.

month.title: CS-Pi: Constraint-Satisfying Flow Policy Sampling
month.abstract: A flow-matching policy deployed in the field must often satisfy a constraint that was absent from its demonstrations, such as avoiding an obstacle it has never seen. Retraining for every new constraint is impractical, so the constraint must be enforced at inference time. Enforcing it must not discard what the policy learned: an action the policy would rarely sample may avoid the obstacle yet fail the task. We therefore want actions that are both safe, satisfying the constraint, and plausible, remaining likely under the policy. Gradient guidance, the most common approach, steers noisy states, so it must evaluate its cost on the policy's running estimate of the clean action; when the policy is uncertain between passing left or right of an obstacle, this estimate is their average and can pass straight through it. We instead build on rejection and projection. Rejection redraws actions until one is safe: every output is plausible, but the wait is intractable when safe actions are rare. Projection moves an action to the nearest safe one: it is efficient, but the result need not be plausible. Our key insight is that flow-matching sampling lets us combine the two, keeping projection's efficiency and rejection's plausibility. CS-Pi, our draw-project-renoise sampler, projects each draw to the nearest safe action, adds noise back scaled to how far the projection moved it, and re-runs the unmodified policy until a draw is safe. Replacing only the projection step extends CS-Pi to continuous costs. Across a 2D diagnostic, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, an orientation preference, and a zero-shot Franka deployment, CS-Pi reaches 81% safe success on the shelf and 55% on hardware, against 55% and 40% for projection, while staying plausible.
month.tldr: CS-Pi enforces unseen inference-time constraints on flow policies via draw-project-renoise sampling that stays plausible under the policy.
month.summary: Gradient guidance fails on multimodal policies (averaging can pass through obstacles), rejection is slow and projection is implausible. CS-Pi projects each draw to the nearest safe action, renoises proportionally to the projection distance, and reruns the unmodified flow policy until safe. It reaches 81% safe success on a shelf pick-and-place and 55% on a Franka vs 55% and 40% for projection.
month.why: Clean, usable idea for constrained sampling from flow-matching policies.

month.title: Coupled Guidance for Flow Matching
month.abstract: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.
month.tldr: Shows naive diffusion-style guidance breaks flow matching's coupling distribution and proposes Coupled Guidance derived geometrically for flow models.
month.summary: Theoretical analysis reveals translated diffusion guidance violates the training coupling, weakening control. Coupled Guidance respects the coupling, giving more stable steering, with applications to stochastic robotic controllers and image synthesis.
month.why: Guidance theory for flow matching with robotics use, a core interest.

month.title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
month.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.
month.tldr: Studies SFT recipes for pi0.5 on a LEAP hand before DSRL steering; best SFT checkpoint is rarely most steerable.
month.summary: With few demos and two sim tasks, five fine-tuning recipes are compared: SFT success poorly predicts post-DSRL success, freezing the VLM and tuning the action expert is most steerable, and LoRA is least steerable.
month.why: Directly combines VLA fine-tuning, dexterous hands, and diffusion steering RL.

month.title: SimDuoReal: Object-Centric Bimanual Policy for Emergent Dexterity
month.abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires coordinated arm and hand control, yet specifying such coordination manually is challenging and often task-specific. In this work, we explore whether complex bimanual dexterity can emerge from a simple object-centric learning objective. We train reinforcement learning policies under a shared object-centric reward, varying their training environments rather than tuning separate rewards for each behavior. We find that the policies discover pre-grasp manipulation, grasping and regrasping, in-hand adjustment and handover to reach object-pose goals without hand-designed motion sequences. We then refine the experts on transition states and use DAgger and reinforcement learning to distill them into a single policy that composes these behaviors for diverse bimanual tasks. On real hardware, the same policy succeeds in 61 of 80 trials (76.3\%) across four tasks with unseen objects and no task-specific fine-tuning. In simulated barcode scanning, our policy achieves 85.0\% success, compared with 60.4\% for two single-arm policies without handover. These results suggest that this objective provides a simple and scalable interface for learning general bimanual dexterity, shifting the burden from manually designing robot coordination to specifying what should happen to the object.
month.tldr: SimDuoReal shows bimanual dexterous behaviors (regrasp, in-hand adjustment, handover) emerge from one object-centric RL reward, distilled into one real-world policy.
month.summary: Hand-designing bimanual arm-hand coordination is task-specific. RL policies trained with a shared object-pose reward across varied environments discover pre-grasp, regrasp, in-hand adjustment and handover; experts are refined on transitions and distilled with DAgger and RL into a single policy. On hardware it succeeds in 61/80 (76.3%) trials across four tasks with unseen objects, and 85.0% vs 60.4% on sim barcode scanning.
month.why: Squarely in core interests: emergent bimanual dexterity with sim-to-real.

month.title: GSBR: Geometric Support Behavior Regularization for Online RL
month.abstract: Regularizing online reinforcement learning (RL) toward a pretrained base policy can improve sample efficiency and learning stability, but regularization that is too restrictive limits how much the policy can improve. Base policies -- typically diffusion or flow-matching models trained by imitation learning on large, diverse datasets -- capture many behaviors that are reasonable but suboptimal.
