Existing regularizers using such base policies are too restrictive in one of two ways: behavioral cloning regularizers pull the actor toward the full base-policy distribution, penalizing it for discarding suboptimal modes, while hard support constraints forbid improvements that lie just outside the base policy's support. We propose Geometric Support Behavior Regularization (GSBR), which penalizes actions by their distance from the base policy's support. Actions within the support incur no penalty, so the actor can concentrate on high-value modes; outside the support, where value estimates are less reliable, the penalty grows smoothly with distance while still permitting improvement when the value gained outweighs the penalty. GSBR estimates this distance from a finite set of base-policy samples, so it requires only sample access to the base policy. Across 19 tasks on four robotic benchmarks, GSBR raises the average success rate from 33% for the base policy to 95%, achieving the highest average success rate and throughput among all compared methods, with about 23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method. Project website and open-source code at https://charlesxu0124.github.io/gsbr/ .
month.tldr: GSBR regularizes online RL by distance to a diffusion/flow base policy's support rather than its full distribution.
month.summary: BC regularizers penalize dropping suboptimal modes while hard support constraints block nearby improvements. GSBR applies zero penalty inside the base policy's support and a smoothly growing penalty outside, estimated from base-policy samples only. Across 19 tasks on four benchmarks, raises success from 33% to 95% with ~23% higher normalized throughput than the next-best RL method.
month.why: Levine-group method for RL fine-tuning of generative BC policies, squarely in your core interests.

month.title: Beyond Validation Loss: Coverage and Reliability Dynamics in Robot Policy Pretraining
month.abstract: In modern robot learning, generative robot policies are first pretrained through supervised learning from demonstrations, then refined through reinforcement learning, supervised finetuning, or other forms of posttraining. Yet conventional pretraining metrics, such as validation loss and average task success, provide an incomplete account of which policies support both effective direct deployment and subsequent posttraining. In this work, we study closed-loop pass@k, which evaluates the probability that k rollouts from the same initial condition attain at least one success. Thus, pass@1 measures mean task success; large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable under repeated sampling. Across a wide range of posttraining recipes, we show that large-k pass@k reveals posttraining differences not captured by pass@1. In particular, checkpoints with similar pass@1 but different large-k pass@k have different posttraining performance. Moreover, we show pass@k peaks at different checkpoints during supervised pretraining, revealing a coverage-reliability tradeoff over the course of training. Based on these observations, we propose two practical interventions: (1) a purely offline checkpoint-selection criterion that balances coverage and reliability without closed-loop evaluation, and (2) a generative data augmentation procedure that expands supervision beyond the finite demonstration set, preserving large-k pass@k while maintaining or improving pass@1 and raising the observed coverage-reliability Pareto frontier. Together, our results motivate evaluation, checkpoint selection, and training procedures that explicitly account for posttraining. Blog post, visualizations, and code are available at https://zhanyisun.github.io/robot-policy-learning-dynamics/.
month.tldr: Shows closed-loop pass@k reveals a coverage-reliability tradeoff in generative policy pretraining that predicts post-training success.
month.summary: Argues validation loss and mean success miss what matters for post-training. Large-k pass@k distinguishes checkpoints with equal pass@1 but different RL/SFT post-training outcomes, and peaks at different points in pretraining. Proposes an offline checkpoint-selection criterion and generative data augmentation that preserves coverage while raising pass@1.
month.why: Rigorous understanding paper (Simchowitz, Song) directly on BC pretraining for RL fine-tuning of generative policies.

month.title: How Much of Your VLA Is kNN
month.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.
month.tldr: Shows kNN retrieval of demo action chunks reaches 91.7% on LIBERO, and that fine-tuned VLAs mostly act as better retrieval keys.
month.summary: It's unclear how much LIBERO success needs generalization. Retrieval without training reaches 91.7% and degrades least under LIBERO-Plus; across nine VLAs, fine-tuning mainly makes the backbone a better retrieval key with actions staying close to demos. A Local Action Consistency metric tracks retrieval success and can guide key training.
month.why: Important 'understanding' paper questioning what VLAs and benchmarks measure.

month.title: TouchBridge: Tactile-Conditioned Human-to-Robot Transfer for Dexterous Manipulation
month.abstract: Human demonstrations offer an efficient and scalable source of data for dexterous robot manipulation, but differences in sensing and hand morphology complicate the transfer of contact-rich interactions. We present TouchBridge, a hardware--software co-designed framework for human-to-robot data transformation. A wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robot interface establish cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and fingertip tactile sensing. We introduce Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to align fingertip contact patches and preserve their spatial relations within and across hands. Unlike object-aware or simulation-based transfer pipelines, Tac-Retarget requires no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation for retargeting, enabling direct and scalable conversion of human demonstrations into robot-domain training data. Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a 72.5% average success rate, compared with 77.5% using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstration collection is 7.0x faster. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.
month.tldr: TouchBridge co-designs wearable and robot tactile interfaces and Tac-Retarget to convert human dexterous demonstrations into robot data by aligning fingertip contact patches.
month.summary: Sensing and morphology gaps hamper human-to-robot dexterous transfer. Matched visual and fingertip-tactile interfaces on human and robot establish correspondence, and Tac-Retarget uses measured contact to align fingertip patches and their spatial relations, requiring no object mesh, pose estimate or simulation.
month.why: Tactile-conditioned retargeting of human data for dexterous hands is a core interest.

month.title: CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation
month.abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand--contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on $43$--$78\%$ of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on $<10\%$ and $22.5\%$ of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12\% to 32\% on GRAB dataset. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
month.tldr: CARD retargets human hand demonstrations from video, mocap, or tactile gloves to robot actions while preserving explicit contact-force targets.
month.summary: Kinematic retargeting ignores contact dynamics crucial for dexterous success. CARD unifies human data sources via a shared hand-contact representation, outputs contact force targets alongside kinematics without simulator or object models, and uses a tactile tracking controller to maintain contacts during open-loop hardware replay.
month.why: Contact-aware retargeting of human data to dexterous hands is squarely my core interest.

month.title: TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control
month.abstract: Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model's latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at https://tapestry-wam.github.io.
month.tldr: TAPESTRY repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer as a policy by tokenizing actions as single video patches in the shared backbone.
month.summary: Using video models for control usually requires test-time video generation or from-scratch action heads. TAPESTRY linearly projects each action timestep into the VAE patch space so the same patchify layers and transformer process actions, trained with three diffusion objectives and no video generation at inference.
month.why: Elegant unified video-action model design, a stated interest.

month.title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
month.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/
month.tldr: DexDuet learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterous RL policies from a single human demo with interaction rewards and an assisted curriculum.
month.summary: Object-tracking rewards let robots contact wrong parts or slide fingers. DexDuet adds two interaction rewards preserving human hand-object contacts, factorizes bimanual control into weight-sharing per-hand policies conditioned on each other, and uses assisted reference-state initialization. It is evaluated across four bimanual benchmarks.
month.why: Bimanual dexterity from human demonstrations with RL is exactly my core area.

month.title: TouchTwin: Scaling Human Touch Data via Real-to-Sim-to-Real
month.abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31x the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55x. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99x the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.
month.tldr: Rebuilds human demos with an 880-taxel glove in MuJoCo so dexterous policies learn correct contact forces, closing a vision-only 'force gap'.
month.summary: Vision-based real-to-sim-to-real recovers hand motion but not touch: pose imitation grips at 0.31x recorded force and physics replay at 1.55x. TouchTwin reconstructs TouchScale recordings (head/wrist RGB-D plus tactile glove) in MuJoCo with agent-written physics-tested objects and a per-subject tactile hand replaying recorded touch, scaling human touch data for dexterous policies.
month.why: Human hand data plus tactile sensing plus sim-to-real for hands: core.

month.title: DexRemo: A Force-Sensing Hand Platform and Task Suite for Contact-Rich Removal Manipulation
month.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. Project website: https://dexremo.github.io
month.tldr: A high-force three-finger hand with 3-axis fingertip force sensing plus a nine-scenario real-robot suite for contact-rich removal tasks.
month.summary: Removal manipulation (adhesive detachment, cleaning, occluded retrieval) depends on partially observable contact states. DexRemo expresses fingertip forces in a shared wrist frame and trains ACT policies fusing vision, proprioception, fingertip pose and force; six core tasks benchmark the value of force sensing.
month.why: Contact-rich dexterous hardware + force-aware action-chunking policies, core interests.

month.title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control
month.abstract: Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies. In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect. Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size. We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms. Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
month.tldr: Adapts long-action-chunk policies with off-policy RL by learning only how long to execute each chunk.
month.summary: RL fine-tuning of long-chunk policies is sample-hungry due to high-dimensional chunks. ExRL adds a lightweight adapter predicting execution length per chunk, trained with off-policy RL, giving sample-efficient adaptation across diverse long-chunk policies in sim and real with little tuning.
month.why: Squarely at action chunking + RL fine-tuning of generative policies; simple and usable.

month.title: GUARD: Anomaly-Informed Q-Steering for Generative Robot Policies in Dexterous Manipulation
month.abstract: Generative robot policies based on diffusion and flow matching can model complex, multimodal behaviors, but remain susceptible to covariate shift during closed-loop execution. Existing approaches mitigate such failures through additional demonstrations, policy fine-tuning, or test-time guidance, but often require human intervention, engineered rewards, or other task-specific signals. We introduce GUARD, an anomaly-informed Q-steering framework that leverages the policy's training distribution to construct a dense, failure-anticipatory steering signal. GUARD pairs sparse task rewards with dense anomaly scores learned from policy training data and propagates both through a learned Q-function. Its gradients then steer the denoising process toward actions that improve task return while preventing trajectories from entering poorly supported regions, without directly modifying the pretrained policy. Across four Adroit dexterous manipulation tasks, GUARD achieves average success rates of $96.0\%$ and $80.0\%$ under nominal and perturbed dynamics, outperforming the strongest baseline by $21.0$ and $20.0$ percentage points while maintaining the lowest anomaly score. GUARD further demonstrates direct sim-to-real transfer on in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation tasks, achieving $40$ and $25$ percentage-point gains in success rate. These results demonstrate that anomaly signals can serve not only for failure monitoring but also to complement sparse task rewards as effective supervision for robust policy steering.
month.tldr: GUARD steers diffusion/flow policies with gradients of a Q-function trained on sparse rewards plus dense anomaly scores from the policy's training distribution.
month.summary: Generative policies drift into unsupported states under covariate shift. GUARD learns anomaly scores from training data, propagates them with sparse task rewards through a Q-function, and uses its gradients to steer denoising without modifying the base policy. It reaches 96.0%/80.0% on Adroit under nominal/perturbed dynamics (+21/+20pp) and gains 40 and 25pp on real in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation.
month.why: Q-steering of generative policies for dexterous in-hand tasks with sim-to-real, core RLGen + Dex.

month.title: Contact Imitation Interface: Transferring Dexterous Skills by Showing How Contact Unfolds
month.abstract: Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator's natural dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI), a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces. The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment. CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action representations, improving mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand-task pairs on LEAP and Wuji. Hardware designs and software are publicly available.
month.tldr: CIMI transfers robot-free human dexterous demonstrations via contact-grounded interfaces and a hierarchical contact-surface planner policy.
month.summary: Preserving natural dexterity while producing transferable data is hard. CIMI combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-first retargeting, and a policy where a planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and fingers, improving final-stage success by at least 50 points.
month.why: Contact-centric human-to-robot dexterous transfer, squarely core.

month.title: Dexterous In-Hand Object Pose Reaching with Learned Safety Filters
month.abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.
month.tldr: A sim-only recipe trains LEAP hand policies for long sequences of in-hand object pose reaching at any wrist orientation, with learned safety filters, transferring zero-shot.
month.summary: In-hand skills are usually limited to rotation and drops are rarely measured. The recipe combines diverse resets and goals from generated grasp datasets, an adaptive friction curriculum, and careful system identification, plus learned safety filters to avoid drops; policies transfer zero-shot to a real LEAP hand.
month.why: Sim-to-real in-hand reorientation beyond rotation with safety analysis; core dexterity work.

month.title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
month.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.
month.tldr: Systematic study of what makes chunked VLAs (pi0.5) reactive in dynamic manipulation: horizons, async inference, continuity, adaptation.
month.summary: On two dynamic sim benchmarks and three real tasks, the best prediction horizon is ~1 s, short horizons help more with async execution, and trajectory-continuity methods beat pure latency reduction. Changing execution horizon matched RL adaptation gains on a conveyor task.
month.why: Rigorous empirical guidance on action chunking and real-time chunk execution.

month.title: Explicitly capturing demonstrator multi-modality for distillation into diffusion policies
month.abstract: The diversity of a distilled diffusion policy's outputs matters beyond how it impacts the policy's success rate. In particular, downstream applications like test-time search and policy improvement require exploration. Thus, we want to distill multi-modal demonstrators into diffusion policies which reproduce their conditional action distributions. Standard data collection for behavior cloning applies a sliding window to demonstration episodes, which pairs unique observation histories with actions. These datasets can be fit by a policy that is either multi-modal, or unimodal with high Lipschitz constant to capture a diversity of actions seen at nearby observation samples. Prior work finds that diffusion policies trained on sparse data learn the latter, memorizing one action per observation. We adapt vine sampling to behavior cloning data collection to resolve this ambiguity: at some states the demonstrator visits, query it $k$ times from exactly the same observation. On a synthetic task, we study how the number of actions per observation, $k$, affects the learned policy, and find that larger $k$ yields a policy that better matches the demonstrator's conditional distribution, including its multi-modality and diversity. On a 2D truck unloading task, vine sampling likewise leads to a policy closer to the demonstrator and substantially improves both best-of-$N$ and expert iteration performance.
month.tldr: Vine sampling (querying the demonstrator k times from the same state) makes distilled diffusion policies truly multimodal rather than memorizing one action per observation.
month.summary: Sliding-window BC data can be fit by a high-Lipschitz unimodal policy, so diffusion policies memorize. Querying the demonstrator multiple times from identical observations resolves this; larger k better matches the conditional distribution on a synthetic task. On 2D truck unloading it yields a closer policy and substantially improves best-of-N and expert iteration.
month.why: Sharp insight on diffusion policy multimodality vs memorization, relevant to RL fine-tuning and search.

month.title: TactileLab: Sim-to-Real Dexterous Robot Manipulation with Efficient Shear-Sensitive Tactile Simulation
month.abstract: Robotic simulators that represent shear within tactile sensing are becoming increasingly important for contact-rich manipulation. However, simulating contact shear with high-fidelity deformable or soft-body simulation is computationally demanding, limiting scalability to large-scale reinforcement learning. Here we introduce \textit{TactileLab}, a scalable multimodal tactile simulation framework built on IsaacLab, with a particular focus on a new optical-flow-based tactile representation termed \textit{simulated tactile flow}. Instead of relying on soft-body physics to model shear deformation, TactileLab uses rigid-body simulation to efficiently estimate dense tangential motion at the contact interface, producing tactile flow fields that encode shear-relevant contact dynamics. This flow field complements geometric features from a contact depth field. We further introduce a novel policy architecture for jointly processing long-horizon proprioceptive signals and rich tactile observations. Across multiple contact-rich tasks, policies trained using simulated tactile flow learn efficiently at scale and exhibit emergent contact-aware behaviours. To facilitate sim-to-real policy deployment, we then propose a novel real-to-sim tactile translation method that maps real tactile image streams to simulated tactile flow and depth fields, together with a new tactile data collection method, and validate it across diverse tactile sensor designs. Using this pipeline, we demonstrate real-world deployment on tasks encompassing dual-arm and dexterous in-hand manipulation. Overall, TactileLab provides an end-to-end sim-to-real framework for scalable tactile policy learning, enabling diverse shear-sensitive manipulation across heterogeneous tactile robotic systems.
month.tldr: TactileLab adds rigid-body 'tactile flow' shear simulation to IsaacLab for scalable RL, plus real-to-sim tactile translation for sim-to-real dexterous manipulation.
month.summary: Simulating tactile shear with soft-body physics is too slow for large-scale RL. TactileLab estimates dense tangential contact motion from rigid-body sim as a 'tactile flow' field alongside contact depth, pairs it with a long-horizon proprio+tactile policy architecture, and maps real tactile images to simulated flow/depth. Policies show emergent contact-aware behavior and deploy on real dual-arm and in-hand dexterous tasks across several sensor designs.
month.why: Directly on target: scalable shear-aware tactile sim and sim-to-real for in-hand dexterity.

month.title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
month.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.
month.tldr: Bimanual VLA trained on 16,151 hours of handheld-gripper demos with no robot data, reaching 78% on ten long-horizon real tasks.
month.summary: Collects data with YUBI, an open-source handheld gripper, and trains a wrist-camera-only model that learns task-relevant view regions, predicts task stage, and streams actions. Averages 78% vs 27% for the best of four VLAs post-trained on the same demos at an unseen site, across multiple embodiments. Releases dataset, weights and a recipe post-trainable in under four hours on 8 H200s.
month.why: Major open data/model release showing robot-free human data can scale precise manipulation.

month.title: From Teleoperation to Long-Horizon Dexterity: Evaluating Visuomotor Skills and Offline Proxies for Dexterous Manipulation
month.abstract: Imitation learning policies are intended to make robotic manipulation robust to variations in object pose, appearance, and environment that challenge pre-programmed motion. However, real-world performance remains difficult to predict, as conventional optimization signals such as validation loss show no consistent relationship with robot success. To identify the design choices that govern real-world performance, 281 imitation-learning policies spanning seven policy families were evaluated in approximately 1,700 real-robot trials of RJ45 connector grasping and insertion using a five-fingered robotic hand. Controlled ablations showed that observation and action representations dominated conventional optimizer and sampling choices. For point-cloud policies, region-of-interest cropping, representation in the robot-base frame, and normalization within the point encoder each improved success by 70-100 percentage points. For the vision-language-action policy, absolute rather than relative action prediction improved insertion success by up to 70 percentage points. Skill decomposition, multi-view perception, and recovery demonstrations were associated with the strongest-performing systems, although their effects were not independently isolated. Of 67 offline metrics evaluated, only five measures of predicted-motion smoothness and directness reliably correlated with insertion success (r = -0.70 to -0.80), and only within a single policy family. These results identify representation choices as key determinants of real-world imitation-learning performance and show that offline metrics can shortlist policies, but cannot replace real-robot evaluation.
month.tldr: Evaluates 281 imitation policies across seven families in ~1,700 real trials of five-fingered RJ45 insertion, finding representations dominate and validation loss does not predict success.
month.summary: Validation loss shows no consistent relationship with real success. Controlled ablations show observation and action representations matter more than optimizer or sampling choices; for point-cloud policies, ROI cropping, base-frame representation and encoder normalization each raise success, and offline proxies are assessed.
month.why: Large-scale real-robot dexterous IL study with actionable design insights.

month.title: ODE Policy: Robot Learning via Action Dynamics, Not Actions
month.abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9$\times$ the success, 5.4$\times$ the generalization, and 3.9$\times$ the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8$\times$ faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.
month.tldr: ODE policy learns a neural-ODE vector field over actions, integrating each action from the previous one for continuous trajectories.
month.summary: Instead of predicting action values, a neural ODE learns the action's dynamics by matching integrated actions to targets over short chunks (IL) or single steps (RL), with a diversity head for multimodality. Versus flow matching after one epoch: 5.9x success, 5.4x generalization, 10.8x faster generation; best on 14 real tasks spanning single-arm, bimanual, dexterous and humanoid robots. Also speeds up humanoid motion-tracking RL.
month.why: A direct challenger to flow-matching policies and action chunking with broad real-robot evidence, including dexterous hands.

month.title: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
month.abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.
month.tldr: RoboTryOn converts egocentric human videos into robot videos via 'virtual try-on' and labels actions with a depth-aware IDM.
month.summary: Keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for a target robot specified by a reference image, translating keyframes autoregressively and conditioning on hand skeletons. An inverse dynamics model infers actions from synthesized videos. Raises novel-task success including bimanual from 2% to 60% with no robot demos of those tasks and matches teleop-only training at about a third of the cost.
month.why: Synthetic dexterous data from human video, in line with DreamGen-style ideas you track.

month.title: Beyond Policy Patches: Distilling RL Specialists into Vision-Language-Action Policies
month.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can handle noncritical stages of long-horizon manipulation yet fail during short precision-critical phases. Lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) specialists can address these failures without directly applying RL to the full VLA, but retain auxiliary controllers and switching mechanisms at deployment. We study how to transfer their capabilities into a single flow-matching VLA. Direct imitation of specialist rollouts can reproduce action jitter and leave the VLA unprepared for states encountered during its own execution. We introduce REPAIR, a value-guided distillation framework that combines offline initialization with on-policy refinement. At each critical-phase observation, REPAIR queries the corresponding specialist for multiple action candidates and weights them using its critic to construct a supervision distribution. A shared weighted flow-matching objective trains the VLA first on observations from specialist-assisted rollouts, then on observations collected through its own execution. Specialists provide supervision without taking control during on-policy collection and are removed at deployment. Across six real-robot tasks with 30 evaluation trials per task, REPAIR achieves 100% success on all six tasks, with lower mean end-effector jerk than specialist-assisted execution on every task.
month.tldr: REPAIR distills RL specialists into a single flow-matching VLA via critic-weighted flow matching with offline then on-policy data.
month.summary: VLAs fail in short precision-critical phases where RL specialists help but require switching. REPAIR queries specialists for multiple action candidates, weights them by critic value, and trains with weighted flow matching first on assisted rollouts then on the VLA's own states. Achieves 100% on six real tasks (30 trials each) with lower jerk than specialist-assisted execution.
month.why: Strong real-robot RL+flow-VLA fine-tuning recipe directly on your list.

month.title: Expanding the Quality-Coverage Frontier with Competitive Flow Matching
month.abstract: Flow matching (FM) generators often face a quality-coverage tradeoff. Inference-time techniques such as classifier-free guidance raise quality, but at the cost of coverage. We revisit a basic property of FM -- an intermediate noisy image corresponds to multiple valid targets, which is collapsed into a single mean velocity by design. This can cover multiple modes of the distribution under ideal conditions, but is it optimal in practice? We instead investigate if directly modeling the modes of intermediate states better covers the modes of the full distribution. To do so, we augment the predictor with a randomly drawn low-dimensional code $z$, sampling $K$ candidate velocities for each training sample. We then apply the loss only to the best-matching candidate. This winner-take-all objective enables different codes to specialize and collectively cover different modes. Furthermore, this term naturally enables a new form of guidance, auxiliary conditioning scaling, which complements traditional guidance methods. Together, these two guidance mechanisms show that our method substantially improves the quality--coverage frontier. We validate on ImageNet-256, using two different testbeds, SiT and RAEv2. Given less than 3% of the original SiT pretraining compute for post-training, at the 67% Recall point, our method reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 19.22 to 5.91. On RAEv2, at the 70% Recall point, it reduces $\mathrm{FD}_{r,6}$ from 16.83 to 3.18.
month.tldr: Competitive flow matching adds a latent code with winner-take-all loss over K velocity candidates to cover modes, plus a new guidance.
month.summary: Standard FM collapses multiple valid targets into a mean velocity. Sampling K candidates via a low-dim code and training only the best enables mode specialization and 'auxiliary conditioning scaling' guidance. On ImageNet-256 at 67% recall, FD drops from 19.22 to 5.91 on SiT with <3% of pretraining compute.
month.why: New angle on flow-matching mode coverage and guidance, directly in your generative-modeling interests and relevant to multimodal policies.

month.title: Open-HumanWAM: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
month.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanWAM, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanWAM-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanWAM-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.
month.tldr: Open recipe scaling egocentric human-video pretraining of world-action models to 50k hours, finding log-linear scaling to robot success.
month.summary: Curates Open-HumanWAM-50K with hand motion and language annotations; HumanWAM-Vanilla pretrained on human video alone reaches 92.1% on RoboTwin Clean2Clean after post-training. Joint human-robot goal-conditioned pretraining reaches 84.6% on Clean2Random and shows in-context adaptation on real robots. Data, pipelines and checkpoints released.
month.why: Large open resource on learning from egocentric human data via world-action models.

month.title: GRASP: Gradient-Guided Sampling for Contact-Rich Physics-Based Motion Retargeting
month.abstract: We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.
month.tldr: Sampling-plus-recovered-gradient trajectory optimization for physics-based retargeting of human demos to dexterous hands and humanoids.
month.summary: GRASP extends tempered SMC by fitting local quadratic models to archived rollouts and using their gradients for MCMC rejuvenation, without a differentiable simulator; GRASP-MPC scales to long demos. Achieves 92.8% success on 1,352 bimanual OakInk2 demos with a shared tracking objective and improves PPO tracking for pen spinning. Real-hardware dexterous and humanoid demos.
month.why: Directly addresses retargeting human hand data under contact, a core interest.

month.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
month.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.
month.tldr: iWAM conditions the policy on features from a single flow-video-model evaluation using a learned bidirectional flow map instead of generating future frames.
month.summary: Generating futures is too slow for control. iWAM inverts training futures into noise latents via flow-matching reversibility and learns a bidirectional flow map so one forward pass gives informative conditioning features. Recovers WAM generalization in sim and real at much lower inference cost.
month.why: A principled flow-map idea from Simchowitz's group linking generative-model theory and world-action policies.

month.title: OVOGO: Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
month.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning while inexpensive generative sampling supports policy optimization, providing an effective approach to experience-based post-training of flow-based VLAs.
month.tldr: OVOGO does offline RL for flow VLAs by separating offline critic learning from on-policy resampling of the generative process.
month.summary: Collecting new robot interactions for flow-VLA improvement is costly, but fresh generation trajectories can be resampled cheaply at replay observations. OVOGO learns a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic combining in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, then optimizes the flow policy on-policy over generated actions. It improves flow VLAs from logged experience.
month.why: Offline RL fine-tuning of flow-matching policies is a core RL+generative topic.

month.title: EgoStudy: How Does Scaling Egocentric Data Affect VLA and WAM Pretraining?
month.abstract: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.
month.tldr: EgoStudy runs controlled experiments on how egocentric human data scale, diversity and processing affect VLA and world-action-model pretraining.
month.summary: The value of egocentric human data for robots is unclear due to embodiment gaps. Holding robot data fixed, they vary egocentric scale, diversity, processing and co-training for VLAs and WAMs. Diversity, trajectory alignment and detailed language matter most, with scaling effects differing between VLAs and WAMs.
month.why: Systematic study on learning from human egocentric data, central to dexterous data scaling.

month.title: DelayOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation from a Synchronous Teacher for Real-time Asynchronous Policies
month.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
month.tldr: DelayOPSD distills a synchronous flow-VLA teacher into an asynchronous delayed student on the policy's own rollouts for real-time execution.
month.summary: Asynchronous chunk execution conditions on stale observations; actions differ little on expert data but diverge on the policy's own delayed rollouts. DelayOPSD trains the delayed student, seeing an earlier frame plus pending actions, to imitate the synchronous teacher on on-policy rollouts. This recovers performance under latency.
month.why: Directly addresses real-time/asynchronous action chunking, a core interest.

month.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
month.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_0,π_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $π_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.
month.tldr: JKO-GRPO augments Flow-GRPO for flow-matching VLAs with Wasserstein proximal (JKO) steps using transport targets from group advantages.
month.summary: Flow-GRPO and pi_RL reweight sampled actions by advantage but ignore distances between them. JKO-GRPO treats each state's action group as an empirical distribution, builds transport targets via a soft discrete c-transform of group-relative advantages, and regresses the deterministic flow sampler onto them alongside clipped Flow-GRPO without KL. It improves RL fine-tuning of pi0/pi0.5-style VLAs.
month.why: RL fine-tuning of flow VLAs with optimal transport is a core RL+generative-policy topic.

month.title: Distilling Touch into Vision-Only Policies for Contact-Rich Manipulation
month.abstract: Tactile feedback benefits contact-rich manipulation, yet deploying tactile sensors introduces additional hardware and maintenance requirements. Tactile experience can still provide effective supervision for policies that operate without tactile sensors at deployment. Tactile imagination methods such as TacImag remove this hardware dependency by predicting tactile observations, but retain a reconstruction stage whose errors can propagate into action generation. We present TacitTouch, a distillation framework that transfers tactile-guided behavior directly into a vision-only policy. The core shift is from "learn to imagine what touch would feel like" to "learn to behave as if you could feel touch": the student directly learns tactile-guided action patterns without reconstructing tactile observations. A frozen visuotactile teacher supervises the student's denoising predictions and intermediate action representations at the same noisy action and flow time. Training also uses demonstrated-action supervision. Deployment retains only the visual policy, with no tactile encoder, expert, or generator. Across four simulated UniVTAC tasks and four real-world tasks, TacitTouch achieves absolute improvements of 16.0% and 22.5% in mean success rate over vision-only control, respectively. The absolute gaps to the teacher using measured tactile input are only 2.0% and 3.75%, respectively. In robustness tests, it also outperforms TacImag, with absolute gains of up to 20.0% in mean success rate. Project page: https://pier-lab.github.io/tacittouch/
month.tldr: TacitTouch distills a visuotactile diffusion/flow teacher into a vision-only student by matching denoising predictions and action features.
month.summary: Tactile sensors add hardware burden, and tactile-imagination methods propagate reconstruction errors. TacitTouch has a frozen visuotactile teacher supervise the vision-only student's denoising predictions and intermediate action representations at matched noisy action and flow time, so the student behaves as if it could feel touch. It targets contact-rich manipulation without tactile sensors at deployment.
month.why: Combines tactile sensing, contact-rich manipulation and flow/diffusion policy distillation, all core interests.

month.title: DUO Policy: Bridging Human Video Coverage and Robot Precision for Fine-Grained Manipulation
month.abstract: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. Project Webpage: https://mingxi-jia.github.io/duo_policy_site/
month.tldr: DUO Policy splits a skill into a human-video-pretrained hand policy for free-space motion and a robot policy for precise corrections, with a learned gate.
month.summary: Co-training on human and robot data treats sources as equally useful everywhere. DUO observes human data helps where precision demands are low, while robot data matters near precision-critical states; it uses a hand policy from human video, a robot policy from sparse in-hand data, and a gate learned from interventions. This enables fine-grained tasks like insertion with little robot data.
month.why: Clear insight on leveraging human video for precise manipulation, a core interest.

month.title: SHAPE: Discrete Supervision and Parallel Continuous Streams for Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Human Data
month.abstract: Egocentric human recordings are far cheaper than dexterous robot demonstrations, promising stronger pretraining and direct skill learning without task-specific robot data. Yet humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics, so human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies, providing only retargeted end-effector (EEF) actions. This raises two questions: how human data should supervise the policy, and how a dexterous robot should read out actions at deployment. We address both in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), a vision-language-action (VLA) model whose backbone predicts discrete action tokens of EEF chunks as an auxiliary task, while a shared flow-matching expert outputs two executable streams, EEF and joint. On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, a matched study shows that discrete supervision helps learn from human data, driving backbone gradients and shaping action-informative representations across domains. Under standard control pipelines at deployment, direct joint readout excels at fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, scoring 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for π0.5, whereas IK-based EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE learns new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.
month.tldr: SHAPE uses discrete EEF action tokens as auxiliary supervision and parallel EEF/joint flow streams to learn dexterity from egocentric human data.
month.summary: On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, discrete supervision helps absorb human data; joint readout scores 0.80 vs 0.63 for pi0.5 on six tasks with robot demos, while EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer, enabling new tasks from human demos alone.
month.why: Human-video-to-dexterous VLA recipe with careful matched study.

month.title: Stochastic Self-Distillation for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
month.abstract: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance in robotics through imitation learning, yet fine-tuning them with on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is limited. In group-based RL methods like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), every rollout step requires multi-step ODE integration, and the sampler's limited stochasticity leads to rollout groups with low variance. We propose VLA-SSD, which addresses both high inference latency and limited stochasticity. In particular, our method self-distills a pretrained flow-matching action head into a stochastic one-step policy by conditioning a single-jump generator on a Brownian path. We derive a conditional action density via our stochastic one-step policy, enabling efficient post-training via likelihood-ratio RL algorithms. We show that distilling VLA-SSD from the $π_0$ VLA reduces the action head's forward-pass time by a factor of 7.7, at the cost of a 5.5% relative decrease in the success rate on the LIBERO benchmark. However, by leveraging the increased sample diversity of VLA-SSD during group generation, post-training a $π_{0.5}$ VLA using GRPO yields a 20.6% relative improvement.
month.tldr: Self-distills a flow VLA head into a stochastic one-step policy with tractable density for efficient GRPO fine-tuning.
month.summary: VLA-SSD conditions a single-jump generator on a Brownian path, deriving a conditional action density for likelihood-ratio RL. Distilled from pi0 it cuts head time 7.7x at a 5.5% relative success drop on LIBERO, and GRPO on pi0.5 yields a 20.6% relative improvement thanks to more diverse groups.
month.why: Directly addresses RL fine-tuning of flow policies and one-step generation.

month.title: Conditional Optimal Transport and Triangular Maps for Imitation Learning
month.abstract: We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.
month.tldr: Frames imitation as triangular transport from an empirical action-chunk reference, giving OT, flow-matching, and stochastic-interpolant policies.
month.summary: Diffusion Policy fixes a Gaussian source; this work makes the reference distribution a design choice by casting policies as the second block of a triangular transport map, using the empirical demo action-chunk distribution as source. Three instances (OTP, FMP, SIP) match Diffusion/Consistency Policy on Push-T and robomimic Square with much smaller networks; OTP produces a chunk in one evaluation of a 0.23M-parameter net.
month.why: Directly relevant to source-distribution choice and few-step generative policies, tying stochastic interpolants to IL.

month.title: DexFormer 2.0: Towards a Cross-Embodiment Foundation Policy for Dexterous Grasping
month.abstract: Dexterous grasping policies are usually trained for one arm paired with one hand. Every new pairing then needs its own policy, and the number of policies grows with every arm and hand added. We ask whether a single policy can control many arm-hand combinations and transfer to pairings and hands it has never seen. This is hard because robots differ in the number, layout, and dynamics of their joints, so their observations and actions share no common interface. We present DexFormer 2.0, a single reinforcement learning policy for cross-embodiment dexterous grasping. It maps every robot to a canonical joint interface with validity masks, encodes each joint's morphology with attention biased by the kinematic tree, and uses a Transformer-XL memory to infer embodiment-dependent dynamics from recent interaction. Trained on 18 combinations of four arms and six hands, it reaches 89% stable success on seen combinations and 51% on six held-out arm-hand pairs, outperforming GRU and DexFormer 1.0 baselines. Without fine-tuning, it also grasps with four new hand types and, through retargeting, with parallel grippers. Ablations show that memory, the kinematic-tree bias, and broader pairing coverage each matter for transfer. On a physical Flexiv arm, distilled students transfer zero-shot from simulation with two hands, including a held-out pair. Project website: https://davidlxu.github.io/dexformer2-web/.
month.tldr: Single Transformer-XL RL policy for dexterous grasping across 18 arm-hand pairs, transferring to unseen hands and real robots.
month.summary: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasping is addressed with a canonical joint interface with validity masks, kinematic-tree-biased attention, and Transformer-XL memory to infer dynamics. Trained on 4 arms x 6 hands it gets 89% seen / 51% held-out-pair success, grasps with 4 new hands zero-shot, and distilled students transfer zero-shot to a real Flexiv arm.
month.why: Cross-embodiment sim-to-real for multi-fingered hands, a core interest.

month.title: DAPPT: Domain-Aware Policies from Procedural Trajectories for Sim-to-Real Dexterous Tool Use
month.abstract: Sim-to-real RL has achieved impressive results in dexterous manipulation but remains limited to tasks with accurate rigid-body simulation. However, these methods cannot be applied to skills that involve deformable and particles, with which the simulation speed will become too slow for large-scale RL learning. We present DAPPT, a sim-to-real framework for end-to-end dexterous tool-use manipulation skills, e.g., sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, without simulating non-rigid materials. Our method learns a domain-aware RL policy by tracking procedural trajectories parameterized by domain parameters, and distills it into an end-to-end domain-aware sensorimotor policy. Furthermore, explicit domain represen-tation enables fast selection of domain parameters that can maximize downstream task performance. We evaluate DAPPT end-to-end on six dexterous manipulation tasks, including sand scooping, play-dough rod-rolling, sand scraping, mouse-wheel scrolling, dispenser pressing, and spray triggering. Our method achieves 1.5-3.8x in task metrics through the best domain parameter and transfers zero-shot to the real world.
month.tldr: DAPPT learns sim-to-real dexterous tool use with deformables by tracking procedural trajectories conditioned on domain parameters, without simulating materials.
month.summary: Dexterous tasks with sand or play-dough are too slow to simulate for RL. DAPPT trains domain-aware RL policies tracking parameterized procedural trajectories, distills them into sensorimotor policies, and selects domain parameters to maximize task metrics; across six tasks (scooping, rod rolling, spray triggering, etc.) it gives 1.5-3.8x task metrics and zero-shot real transfer.
month.why: Clever sim-to-real recipe extending dexterous RL to non-rigid tool use (Jia Deng group).

month.title: Behavioral Denoising: A New Perspective on Nonlinear Behavioral Control Inspired by Closed-Form Diffusion Policies
month.abstract: Diffusion policies have become a dominant approach to imitation learning in robotics. Recent work suggests that, in the low-data regime, they largely retrieve or combine the demonstrated actions, which the closed-form diffusion policy does explicitly. This closely resembles behavioral control, where future inputs are formed as linear combinations of recorded trajectories. In this work, we make this connection precise: we show that the weights with which the closed-form diffusion policy combines the demonstrated actions are the unique solution of a regularized behavioral control problem. Building on this connection, we propose an algorithm, termed $χ^2$-projected behavioral denoising, which is a training-free method that combines nearby trajectory data with a limit on extrapolation when the data offer little support. It shows encouraging results on four nonlinear control tasks compared to recent nonlinear behavioral control methods. We hope that this connection offers a useful perspective for understanding both data-driven control and diffusion policies.
